item.title: When Trick or Treat Turns Into Trick or Trouble
item.description:
STORY AT-A-GLANCE

  • Halloween candy can be risky for dogs and cats because chocolate, xylitol, raisins, and sugary treats can cause anything from stomach upset to poisoning
  • Xylitol is especially dangerous for dogs because even a small amount can cause a rapid blood sugar crash, seizures, and serious liver damage
  • Chocolate risk depends on the type, amount eaten, and your pet’s size, with dark and baking chocolate posing the greatest danger
  • Hard candy, gummies, wrappers, and lollipop sticks can also cause choking or intestinal blockages, even when the candy itself is not toxic
  • Keeping candy out of reach, checking sugar-free labels, and calling your veterinarian quickly after suspected exposure can help keep Halloween safer for pets

Halloween is one of the most exciting times of the year. Costumes, decorations, and trick-or-treating are all part of the fun, and for many families, that also means bringing home bags full of candy.

If you share your home with a dog or cat, however, those sweet treats deserve a closer look. Many Halloween favorites contain compounds that can make pets seriously ill, while others create hazards that have nothing to do with the candy itself. Knowing which treats are most concerning can help you avoid an unexpected trip to the veterinarian.

Ingredients That Could Send Your Pet to the Vet

Many of the treats that show up during Halloween are perfectly fine for people but genuinely dangerous for dogs and cats. According to the Animal Medical Center of Cascades, chocolate contains theobromine and caffeine, two stimulant compounds that belong to a group called methylxanthines.1 A person's body clears these out easily, but a dog's or cat's body cannot process them nearly as well, which allows them to build up and affect the heart and nervous system.

Sugar-free candy and gum can be just as concerning. The Amador Valley Veterinary Center explains that many of these products contain xylitol, an artificial sweetener that tricks a dog's body into releasing a flood of insulin, causing blood sugar levels to crash.2

Candy Bowl Culprits to Watch Out For

Understanding why ingredients like chocolate and xylitol are dangerous is a good first step. The next step is knowing which treats are most likely to cause trouble if they end up in your pet's mouth:3,4,5,6

  • Chocolate — Dark chocolate and baking chocolate contain far more theobromine than milk chocolate does, which makes them the most dangerous form. Pure white chocolate has no caffeine or theobromine, but can contribute to gastrointestinal upset due to the fat and sugar content. Symptoms of methylxanthine poisoning can include vomiting, diarrhea, restlessness, a racing heart, tremors, and in severe cases, seizures.
  • Chocolate-covered raisins — These are double trouble. They combine chocolate's toxins with raisins, which have been linked to sudden kidney failure in dogs even in small amounts.
  • Sugar free candy and gum — Xylitol does not just hide in gum. It also shows up in some peanut butter, mints, and baked goods. For a small dog, as little as one piece of sugar free gum can be enough to trigger a dangerous blood sugar crash, with symptoms like weakness, wobbliness, and even seizures showing up within 30 minutes to two hours. Liver damage can follow a day or two later, which is why xylitol is treated as a true emergency even when a dog seems fine at first.
  • Candy corn and other high sugar treats — These will not poison your pet, but a large amount of sugar or fat can upset their stomach or, in dogs prone to it, trigger a painful (and possibly life-threatening) inflammation of the pancreas called pancreatitis. Some brands also use xylitol, so the label is always worth a quick check.
  • Hard candy, gummies, and caramel — These are not toxic, but their size and stickiness make them a choking hazard. If swallowed whole, they can cause a blockage in the intestines serious enough to need surgery.

What Helps Keep Your Pet Out of Trouble

Most Halloween candy mishaps are preventable with a little planning. The American Society for the Prevention of Cruelty to Animals’ (ASPCA) top piece of advice is to stash the treats. A closed cabinet or another secure storage spot works better than a countertop, especially since a curious dog's nose is good enough to sniff out candy left in the open.7

It is also worth paying close attention to products labeled "sugar-free." Xylitol can turn up in gum, mints, baked goods, and even certain peanut butters, so it is worth checking labels before leaving anything within paw's reach.8 Keeping a few pet-safe treats on hand can also make it easier to include your furry family members in the fun without exposing them to unnecessary risk.

Finally, do not overlook the aftermath of the celebration. Cellophane wrappers, lollipop sticks, and other leftovers can pile up quickly once the candy sorting starts, and they are a choking hazard even when the candy itself is harmless.9 Using a trash can with a secure lid can help keep dogs and cats from helping themselves to discarded wrappers and packaging.

When to Consult Your Veterinarian

If you know or even suspect your pet got into chocolate, xylitol, or a large amount of candy, call your vet or a pet poison hotline right away, before symptoms even show up.10 Waiting is the real risk here, especially with xylitol, where damage can move quickly enough that early treatment makes a life-saving difference.

That said, not every stolen piece of candy is an emergency. How worried you should be depends on your pet's size, what kind of candy was eaten, and how much they ate. A large dog that grabs one small piece of milk chocolate is in a very different spot than a small dog that gets into dark chocolate or a handful of sugar-free gum.

Cats are not off the hook either. They tend to be pickier eaters than dogs, but the ASPCA warns that chocolate is just as dangerous for cats, and because they are smaller, it takes even less of it to cause a problem.11

When you do call, have the wrapper or packaging nearby so you can tell your veterinarian exactly what your pet ate and roughly how much. If it happens outside office hours, the ASPCA Animal Poison Control Center and the Pet Poison Helpline are both available around the clock.12

item.title: 3 Commands and 1 Question to Ask Before Traveling with Your Dog
item.description:
STORY AT-A-GLANCE

  • While you may think your dog is adorable no matter what his behavior, if you’re planning to bring him along as a houseguest it’s important that he has some basic manners
  • Before your pet arrives as a guest, be sure he’s housetrained, does not jump up during greetings and knows basic obedience commands like “sit”
  • Always get permission before bringing your pet along on your travels, and be sure the destination is safe and enjoyable for your pet, too
  • Pack a bag for your dog with a first-aid kit, extra collar and ID tag, medical records, bedding, bowls, food and water
  • Never leave your dog in a parked car, even in mild weather, and use proper restraint when traveling by car

Editor's Note: This article is a reprint. It was originally published July 25, 2016.

The majority of Americans view their pets as members of their family, and a sizeable minority likes to bring them along virtually everywhere they can. This may include to pet-friendly restaurants, hotels, work places and yes, even to the homes of friends and family members (sometimes uninvited).

There are pros and cons to bringing your pet “along for the ride.” If your pet struggles with severe separation anxiety, for instance, going with you may save him some serious stress. On the other hand, some pets may find new environments stressful and prefer to stay safely at home.

There are practical considerations, too. Traveling with your pet in the car can be risky, especially if you don’t have proper restraint. And if your pet can’t come inside your destination, such as a grocery store or restaurant, leaving him in your car could be deadly, even if it seems to be mild weather.

However, assuming your dog has the right temperament and personality for an outing, the next factor to consider is his behavior.

A well-socialized, well-behaved dog is a pleasure to be around, but if your dog jumps up on your friends, tracks dirty paw prints across their home, pees on their carpet and barks so loudly that it’s difficult to talk, then, not so much.

3 Commands and Behaviors Your Dog Should Know

While you may think your dog is adorable no matter what his behavior, if you’re planning to bring him along as a houseguest it’s important that he has some manners. The following three commands and behaviors are the bare minimum that your dog should master to ensure he’s invited back again.

  1. Housetraining — A housetraining accident can be embarrassing and annoying if it occurs in someone else’s home. First, realize that even if your dog knows to go potty outside when he’s in his home, those rules may fly out the window when he’s in a new location. The best way to circumvent a mistake is to take your dog outside to go potty as soon as you arrive at your destination.

    Use familiar command words to encourage your dog to do his business, then reward him with a treat or extra praise. When you’re inside, keep a close watch on your dog and take him outside regularly to circumvent any mishaps.

    If you’re new to housetraining your dog, consistency, positive reinforcement and patience are your keys to success. An unattended dog may quickly slip away and go potty indoors, so either clip his leash onto your belt or let him stay in his crate when you can’t give him your full attention.
  2. Jumping — An excited dog may jump up on your friends to say hello. If your friends respond by petting your dog, talking to your dog or even using their hands to remove the dog (which may seem like petting), it reinforces the behavior to your dog. Your dog is looking for interaction, and now he’s received it. If you want to break your dog of this bad habit, ignore the behavior. When your dog jumps up on you, turn your back, stand straight and still and do not acknowledge your dog at all. Instruct your friends and family to do the same.

    Eventually, your dog will realize that jumping isn’t getting him the attention he’s seeking. Another option is to teach your dog the “off” command. If he jumps, give the command, and then reward him once all four paws are touching the floor.
  3. Sit — Before you expect others to accept your dog as your “plus one” on invitations, be sure he knows the “sit” command. This way, if your dog wants to bolt out the door, jump up on furniture or race around the house, you can quickly circumvent these unwanted doggy behaviors with one word: sit. It’s wise to teach basic obedience commands (sit, come, stay, down, etc.) to your dog as soon as your dog arrives — starting the first day you bring him home — but even old dogs can learn these new tricks.

    If you’re having difficulty or your pet doesn’t seem to understand you, solicit the advice of a positive dog trainer to help you communicate more effectively.

Always Ask Before Bringing Your Pet

It’s a good idea for virtually all dogs to know basic housetraining skills and obedience commands (“sit”, “stay”, “come”, “off,” “down” and “drop it”/”leave it”), whether or not you plan to bring him along as a houseguest. However, keep in mind that even a well-behaved pet may not be a welcome addition everywhere you go.

Do not simply assume that your pet will be welcome during your travels, even if your destination appears pet-friendly (such as the home of a friend that also has pets). Your animals may not get along with your friend’s, someone living in the home may be allergic, or there may be other reasons why they’d prefer your pets stay home.

Be sure to get permission first rather than subjecting your pet to travel only to have to turn around and go home. No matter what type of travel you're planning, preparing accordingly ahead of time is key (check out the app BringFido for this).

Identify emergency veterinary clinics along the way, and be sure your hotel or campground allows pets and that you've planned for plenty of pit stops along the way. You should pack a bag for your dog too, including items such as:

  • A basic first-aid kit
  • An extra collar and ID tag
  • Leash
  • A copy of your pet's medical file in print form or on a thumb drive
  • Their dog bed, or towels or blankets for bedding and a couple of favorite toys
  • Bowls, food and treats, along with extra bottled water

Bringing your dog’s crate along is an excellent way to manage unseen issues during your adventure, providing a safe spot in a new location. If your pet enjoys travel, and your destination is pet-friendly, then by all means make the most of these new adventures with your pet.

Sources and References

  • PetMD, 3 Commands Your Dog Needs to Know Before Guests Visit (Archived)

item.title: Is Your Furry Housemate Ready for Cozy Season?
item.description:
STORY AT-A-GLANCE

  • The arrival of fall shifts your cat's sleep, appetite, and grooming habits, so the routine that worked in July may need small adjustments by October
  • Cats shed heavily as they trade a summer coat for a winter one, and all that swallowed fur means more hairballs — regular brushing is the simplest fix
  • Fleas, ticks, and parasite-carrying rodents stay active well into fall, sometimes past the first frost, and indoor-only cats can still be exposed to these pests
  • Autumn brings a specific hazard list: antifreeze from vehicles, rodent bait, moldy leaves, lawn chemicals, late-blooming plants, and open-flame decorations
  • Senior cats feel cold, damp weather in their joints. It is reported that roughly 90% of cats over age 12 show signs of arthritis, which often flares when temperatures drop

You notice the arrival of fall in your own routine first. The sweaters come out; the heater kicks on and fills the house with that faint burnt-dust smell. Remarkably, your cat already felt the change weeks ago.

Two factors drive most of the changes that you will eventually see: less light and less warmth. Shorter days shift your cat's internal clock, and many cats simply sleep more in cooler months. Appetite can also climb, which is an ancestral instinct to stock up before a lean season. The coat starts a full renovation as well, shedding the summer layer to make room for a denser winter one.1,2

A few small adjustments on your end can make the difference between a cat who coasts into winter comfortably and one who spends fall itchy, bored, or sick.

The Fur Situation During Fall

Fall is peak shedding season, and all that fur needs to go somewhere. It lands on your pants, your furniture, and your floor, while some gets swallowed during grooming and can come back up as hairballs.3,4

Brushing is the best thing you can do to help your cat, and it only takes five minutes. Short-haired cats generally do fine with a weekly session; long-haired cats may need daily attention, since their fur mats quickly. Either way, every bit of fur you capture is something your cat will not swallow. While you are brushing, use the time as a health check too, feeling for lumps, scabs, sore spots, or fleas.5,6

For cats who still struggle with hairballs, feeding a wet food diet, feeding fiber-rich food, and offering a hairball supplement can help move swallowed hair through the digestive tract instead of back up, but check with your veterinarian first. That said, spotting the occasional hairball on the floor can be normal; up to twice a month is considered normal. However, retching several times a week, bald patches, or red, irritated skin is not — spotting these means a trip to your veterinarian.7

Shorter Days Can Mean a Bored Cat

Again, your cat sleeps longer hours than humans, more so during fall. But a cat stuck indoors with the windows closed has fewer outlets for their pent-up energy.

Aim for two to three short play sessions a day. Cats hunt in bursts, so 10 focused minutes with a wand toy beats an hour of a toy being ignored. In addition, window perches turn migration season into good sightseeing entertainment for them, and puzzle feeders stretch mealtime while cutting the boredom that leads to overeating. You can also use pesticide-free dry leaves in a shallow box for hiding toys, clean pine cones for batting practice, and small gourds to shove around the floor.8,9,10

If your cat starts asking for more food this month, know that their instinct is real. So is the weight it causes, and keep in mind, obesity remains one of the biggest health problems in house cats. Complications from excess weight gain include diabetes risk, stiff joints, and more difficult grooming, which brings you right back to mats and hairballs.11

If your cat has kidney disease, diabetes, or another ongoing condition, fall is a good time to review the feeding plan before the holidays scramble everyone's routine.12

Fleas and Ticks Do Not Read the Calendar

Fleas and ticks stay active into fall, and in many areas, they are still around after the first frost. As temperatures drop, they actively seek warmth, such as heated houses and warm animals. Fall also brings a rodent surge, which means more chances of parasite infections. And even if your cat never goes outside, fleas can still hitch a ride on your shoes, pant legs, and grocery bags.13,14

That is why year-round prevention is recommended. Ask your veterinarian the appropriate strategy based on your cat's age, weight, and health — and never use a dog product on a cat, since some canine ingredients are deadly to them. For more tips, read “Could Your Pet’s Flea Collar Be Harming Them?”

Fall Is Also the Sneezy Season

Cats get seasonal allergies, too. Common triggers include mold spores from damp leaf piles, pollen from late-blooming plants, and dust stirred up when the furnace runs for the first time in months. At home, clear wet leaf piles near doors and change the furnace filter before you turn on the heat.15,16

The signs do not always look like a human’s seasonal allergies — symptoms may include sneezing or coughing, watery eyes, patchy fur loss, or licking one spot until the fur thins. Those symptoms overlap with fleas and several other conditions, so guessing rarely works. Get your cat examined so you are treating the real, underlying cause.17,18

When the House Gets Busy

If you have several cats, that means more friction during fall, because warm spots become valuable real estate and competition over cozy corners raises tension. Provide more warm resting places than you have cats, keep feeding times regular, and keep up the interactive play.19

Halloween deserves its own warning. Cats are more likely to sustain injury around Halloween than at any other time of year due to increased opportunity for escape, increased exposure to toxins and harmful decor, and due to harm related to Halloween culture itself.20 There is a pervasive belief that black cats in particular may come to harm at Halloween due to being adopted for a Halloween theme and then abandoned, or worse, due to human cruelty. While there is not peer-reviewed evidence supporting this belief, some shelters pause black cat adoptions during the Halloween season because of this possibility.

Black cats are already the least likely color of cat to be adopted out of shelters, and the ASPCA and other humane organizations are working hard to bring awareness to the need for more black cats to be adopted into loving homes. Whether increased risk to black cats is true or not, there is definitely the added stress for cats of a doorbell ringing all evening and heavier holiday traffic. So, keep every cat indoors, set up a quiet room away from the front door with a litter box, water, and a bed, and make sure they are microchipped.21 If your cat is comfortable wearing a collar, you can also consider GPS trackers for added peace of mind.

Thanksgiving brings the same crowd problem. Give your cat a quiet space where they can be alone and brief your guests about foods that are toxic to felines, which include onions and chocolate.22

Every decoration you put out during this season is also new, dangling, and within easy reach for your cat. Examples include:23,24

  • Open flame — Candles and lit jack-o'-lanterns get knocked over, risking burns and fire, and a passing tail can catch a flame
  • Natural decorations — Corn husks, dried flowers, and potpourri can cause stomach upset if chewed and swallowed
  • Cords and strings — Light strands, garlands, tinsel, ribbon, and fake spiderwebs invite chewing and tangling, and swallowed string can cause an intestinal emergency needing surgery
  • Anything small or sharp — Plastic bags, wrappers, and twist ties need to go up high or be stored properly

Warm Beds and a Warm Bathroom

Cats chase warmth with real determination. Kittens cannot regulate their own body temperature for about their first month of life and rely on their mother and littermates for heat, and cats never fully outgrow that habit.

So, give them good options before they invent bad ones. Folded blankets on a sofa, chair, or wicker basket work as well as a store-bought bed. Keep at least one spot away from drafty windows, and for a cat who is always cold, try a bed near a heat vent or a thermal bed made for pets.25,26,27

Apply the same logic to the litter box. A restroom in a cold, drafty corner is something your cat may start avoiding — and that often gets blamed on "behavior" when the real problem is simply the location.28

Older Cats and Cold, Damp Weather

If you have a senior cat, this section matters most. According to Pawsome Vet Care, roughly 90% of cats over 12 years old show signs of arthritis. This is based on a landmark study by Hardie et al. that looked at radiographic (X-ray) evidence of arthritis changes in 100 cats.29 Cold, damp weather tends to make stiff joints worse.30,31

Cats also hide pain well. Instead of limping, an arthritic cat usually just does less: hesitating before jumping, sleeping in new, low spots, stepping just outside the litter box, or looking scruffier.

Here is what you can do to help — give your cat a soft, warm bed away from drafts, and install ramps or steps to their favorite perches. You can also consider adding a night light, since older cats navigate better with a little light, as well as a low-sided litter box. Lastly, you can optimize their nutrition with a focus on joint support — ask your veterinarian about supplements and gentle options like massage, acupuncture, or laser therapy. Twice-yearly exams can also catch age-related problems while they are still manageable.32,33,34

The Fall Hazard List

Most veterinarians recommend keeping cats indoors, and fall is a good illustration of why:35,36

  • Antifreeze — Ethylene glycol is deadly in very small amounts and tastes sweet; while cats do not have sweet receptors, other animals do. Your cat only has to walk through a driveway puddle and groom their paws to ingest a lethal dose.
  • Rodent bait — Rodenticides get used heavily in fall, and cats are poisoned either by eating bait or by catching a rodent that already ate it.
  • Lawn chemicals — These can cling to their fur and paws and get swallowed during grooming. If you treat your yard, water the area afterward.
  • Plants and mushrooms — Chrysanthemums and dahlias are toxic to cats and can cause vomiting and diarrhea, and the wild mushrooms that are poisonous tend to be severely so.
  • Mold and wildlife — Wet, decaying leaf piles grow mold, and animals looking to hibernate can turn aggressive if disturbed.

If you suspect your cat encountered these, call your vet immediately. Do not wait for symptoms.

Set Your Cat Up for a Good Season

Preparing your cat for fall does not have to be challenging. If you are only going to do five things this month, these tips are enough to support their well-being:

  1. Brush your cat — weekly for short coats, daily for long ones — and check their skin while you do.
  2. Keep parasite prevention going. Talk to your veterinarian about natural options that are available.
  3. Swap real candles for flameless, and keep dangling decorations out of reach.
  4. Add a warm, draft-free bed, and make the litter box accessible.
  5. Book a wellness exam, especially if your cat is over 12 or has a chronic condition.

Sources and References

  • 1,5,7,9,11,12,13,15,17,22,23,26,33 North Shore Veterinary Hospital, Fall Cat Care: Keeping Your Feline Happy and Healthy This Season
  • 2,4,6,10,14,16,18,19,21,24,27,28,31,34,36 Arch Creek Animal Clinic, Autumn Cat Care
  • 3,8,25,30,32,35 Pawsome Vet Care, Fall Health & Safety Tips for Cats
  • 20 Animals (Basel). 2020 Sep 23;10(10):1720
  • 29 J Am Vet Med Assoc. 2002 Mar 1;220(5):628-32

So, give them good options before they invent bad ones. Folded blankets on a sofa, chair, or wicker basket work as well as a store-bought bed. Keep at least one spot away from drafty windows, and for a cat who is always cold, try a bed near a heat vent or a thermal bed made for pets.25,26,27

Apply the same logic to the litter box. A restroom in a cold, drafty corner is something your cat may start avoiding — and that often gets blamed on "behavior" when the real problem is simply the location.28

Older Cats and Cold, Damp Weather

If you have a senior cat, this section matters most. According to Pawsome Vet Care, roughly 90% of cats over 12 years old show signs of arthritis. This is based on a landmark study by Hardie et al. that looked at radiographic (X-ray) evidence of arthritis changes in 100 cats.29 Cold, damp weather tends to make stiff joints worse.30,31

Cats also hide pain well. Instead of limping, an arthritic cat usually just does less: hesitating before jumping, sleeping in new, low spots, stepping just outside the litter box, or looking scruffier.

Here is what you can do to help — give your cat a soft, warm bed away from drafts, and install ramps or steps to their favorite perches. You can also consider adding a night light, since older cats navigate better with a little light, as well as a low-sided litter box. Lastly, you can optimize their nutrition with a focus on joint support — ask your veterinarian about supplements and gentle options like massage, acupuncture, or laser therapy. Twice-yearly exams can also catch age-related problems while they are still manageable.32,33,34

The Fall Hazard List

Most veterinarians recommend keeping cats indoors, and fall is a good illustration of why:35,36

  • Antifreeze — Ethylene glycol is deadly in very small amounts and tastes sweet; while cats do not have sweet receptors, other animals do. Your cat only has to walk through a driveway puddle and groom their paws to ingest a lethal dose.
  • Rodent bait — Rodenticides get used heavily in fall, and cats are poisoned either by eating bait or by catching a rodent that already ate it.
  • Lawn chemicals — These can cling to their fur and paws and get swallowed during grooming. If you treat your yard, water the area afterward.
  • Plants and mushrooms — Chrysanthemums and dahlias are toxic to cats and can cause vomiting and diarrhea, and the wild mushrooms that are poisonous tend to be severely so.
  • Mold and wildlife — Wet, decaying leaf piles grow mold, and animals looking to hibernate can turn aggressive if disturbed.

If you suspect your cat encountered these, call your vet immediately. Do not wait for symptoms.

Set Your Cat Up for a Good Season

Preparing your cat for fall does not have to be challenging. If you are only going to do five things this month, these tips are enough to support their well-being:

  1. Brush your cat — weekly for short coats, daily for long ones — and check their skin while you do.
  2. Keep parasite prevention going. Talk to your veterinarian about natural options that are available.
  3. Swap real candles for flameless, and keep dangling decorations out of reach.
  4. Add a warm, draft-free bed, and make the litter box accessible.
  5. Book a wellness exam, especially if your cat is over 12 or has a chronic condition.

item.title: This Self-Mutilating Behavior May Baffle, but It's Truly a Red Flag
item.description:
STORY AT-A-GLANCE

  • Psychogenic alopecia, or excessive grooming in cats, occurs when normal grooming activity becomes obsessive
  • The disorder often begins as a displacement behavior or coping mechanism for kitties dealing with chronic stress
  • Symptoms of this condition include excessive licking, biting, chewing, hair loss, skin wounds and ulcerations
  • Before cats with excessive licking behavior are diagnosed with psychogenic alopecia, medical and environmental causes should be ruled out
  • Treatment for stress-related excessive licking is focused on stress reduction and environmental enrichment

Editor's Note: This article is a reprint. It was originally published December 30, 2018.

Some cats take their natural tendency to groom themselves to the next level, turning it into a compulsion. Kitties who excessively lick and groom themselves have a condition known as psychogenic alopecia, which is one of the most common feline compulsive disorders.

A Common Trigger for This Strange Disorder

Excessive grooming often begins as what’s called a displacement behavior. Cats do best with a daily routine that is predictable and consistent. As a response to a change or stressor in their environment, some kitties begin repetitively performing a specific behavior such as grooming to help reduce the emotional tension they’re feeling.

Licking releases soothing endorphins, so if the anxiety-producing situation is ongoing, the cat may practice the displacement behavior over and over until it becomes compulsive or habitual.

The type of stress that triggers excessive licking tends to be persistent and is often a combination of stressors that are cumulative. For example, a new family member, a move to a new house or even relocating the litterbox can upset the average kitty and trigger displacement behaviors.

Cats at Increased Risk

Female cats tend to be more prone to psychogenic alopecia than males. The disorder can happen at any age, but is commonly seen around the time of puberty. And there may be a genetic basis for this disorder, because it’s seen primarily in certain purebred cats, especially oriental breeds that tend to have anxious temperaments.

The disorder can also develop in kitties who are hospitalized, boarded or otherwise deprived of their freedom (i.e., kenneled for an extended period of time). Bored cats often exhibit the behavior, as well as kitties who are frequently stressed or have an anxious disposition.

Causes of Psychogenic Alopecia

It’s important to differentiate psychogenic alopecia from other reasons kitties lick specific areas of their bodies, such as pain or some type of skin condition. There are actually many medical reasons that cause cats to over-groom. If the problem is generalized itching, the licking will be widespread. If there’s a painful area, the licking will be focused on that spot. Where a cat focuses her licking can give clues as to the underlying issue, which can be any number of things, including:

  • Fleas or other parasites
  • Neurologic or chiropractic issues
  • Food or specific ingredient intolerances
  • A reaction to dust, pollen or mold
  • The presence of environmental toxins (e.g., VOCs, phthalates, scented candles or room sprays or plug-ins, household cleaning chemicals)

Conditions that aren’t skin-related but can cause excessive grooming include cystitis (inflammation of the bladder), hyperthyroidism and anal sac problems.

Identifying and correcting underlying environmental and medical issues is important before assuming your cat is licking for an emotional reason. If a kitty licks to the point of breaking the skin, infection can occur. The presence of infection will intensify the licking, which can result in an even more serious infection and a vicious cycle develops.

How to Distinguish Excessive Grooming from Normal Grooming

Cats spend about 30% to 40% of their day grooming themselves, and much of the remaining time is spent sleeping. That’s why it’s very common for pet parents to be oblivious to the problem until they notice significant hair loss, bald spots or scabs from over-grooming.

It’s also possible cat parents don’t notice the behavior because when they’re home with kitty, she feels more comfortable and relaxed and doesn’t need to self-soothe by licking. Obvious signs of psychogenic alopecia are excessive licking and chewing. More aggressive kitties can resort to biting themselves and pulling out clumps of hair. There may be shafts of hair that are chewed down to stubble; there also can be skin wounds or ulcerations.

In over-grooming situations, hair loss and skin damage will be localized to areas where your cat can reach to lick and chew. Often it’s the abdomen, flank, back, chest or the inner legs. There may also be a line of stubble down the back or on the front of the legs that looks a bit like a “buzz cut.”

In addition to excessive licking, there can be other signs of stress, including hiding, refusing to eat, nervousness or not using the litterbox consistently. However, many kitties with psychogenic alopecia show compulsive grooming as their only symptom of stress.

How to Help a Cat with Psychogenic Alopecia

When all medical issues have been ruled out or resolved and you’ve narrowed the problem down to an issue of compulsive behavioral licking, treatment should be focused on stress reduction and environmental enrichment. Cats like to eat at the same time every day, so make feeding time very consistent. Keep food bowls and litterboxes in the same location and, of course, very clean. Invest in an indoor hunting feeder for your cat.

Provide your kitty with lots of hiding boxes, access to high perches and appropriate scratching surfaces. Most cats enjoy interacting with their humans, so take time every day to be present with your kitty to ensure his emotional and social needs are being met. Also be sure to get your cat physically active every day with interactive toys like a laser pointer or wand toy. Many cats today are bored to the point that it’s unhealthy, so it’s important to provide your kitty with options for mental stimulation throughout the day.

Catios (cat patios) and safe time spent outside can also be wonderful for indoor cats because it allows them to experience the natural world. Open the curtains or blinds before you leave for work so your kitty can see outside. Consider installing window perches and playing kitty videos while you’re away.

Brushing your cat’s coat is beneficial for removing loose hair and cutting down on hairballs, and many kitties really enjoy the attention. Talk to your integrative veterinarian about stress remedies for anxious cats. Flower essences, homeopathics and acupuncture are often used successfully with stressed kitties. Also consider feline facial pheromone sprays such as Feliway. CBD oil can be very beneficial for stressed cats, as can catnip, silver vine and valerian root.

Most importantly, you need to be patient, and please don’t ever punish your cat for over-grooming, as it will only make the situation much worse. Excessive grooming problems take time to resolve, much like any other compulsive behavior. With consistent attention, affection, environmental enrichment and a dependable daily routine, most kitties are able to conquer psychogenic alopecia. They regrow their hair and their quality of life improves within a few months’ time.

item.title: Is This Cheap Ingredient Crowding Out the Good Stuff?
item.description:
STORY AT-A-GLANCE

  • Barley is used in pet foods because it’s cheaper than other ingredients. It’s rich in carbohydrates, and these carb fillers can allow the manufacturer to reduce the amount of meat, which is far more expensive
  • There’s no issue if your pet consumes small amounts of barley, it’s not toxic. Most people resort to adding grains to their pet’s homemade, nutritionally complete food due to finances. Pets don’t need carbs added for nutritional reasons
  • Barley contains gluten, a naturally occurring protein that acts as an antinutrient — this means it interferes with how the body absorbs important minerals and nutrients, so it’s best to limit the amount of grains you feed your pet
  • Once the problem food(s) have been identified, a novel diet should be introduced; for dogs with super-sensitive stomachs, it’s best to avoid all processed pet food in favor of a homemade diet
  • As much as possible, choose organic barley. Conventionally grown barley is often contaminated with glyphosate, a carcinogenic active ingredient found in Roundup and other weedkillers

Editor's Note: This article is a reprint. It was originally published November 21, 2022.

If you’re feeding dog food to your pets and check the ingredients on the label, you might see the word “barley” in the list. Barley, just like rice and other grains, is commonly added to most commercial dog foods, but what is this food actually? Can it provide your pets with notable benefits? Keep reading to discover what barley is, and whether or not it’s a good addition to your pet’s diet.

What Is Barley and Why Is It Used in Pet Foods?

Barley (Hordeum vulgare) belongs to the grass family Poaceae and is known for the edible grain it produces. It’s the fourth largest grain crop grown worldwide, after wheat, rice and corn.1 In the U.S., a large majority of the barley production goes into animal feed and beer manufacturing2 — hence the reason why you’ll see it in some conventional pet foods.

The reason why barley is used in pet foods is because it’s cheaper — it’s rich in carbohydrates, and these carb fillers allow the manufacturer to reduce the amount of meat, which is far more expensive, in their recipes.

Did You Know?

Barley has a long history of use. In ancient Mesopotamia, it was used as a form of currency. Pliny the Elder, a Roman historian, also wrote that in ancient Greece, this food was given to the gladiators, and they’re referred to as “barley eaters.”3

So Is Barley Good for Your Dogs and Cats?

The truth is that barley is a grain, just like wheat and rice. Dogs and cats have no biological need for carbs, and it only converts in their body to sugar. What’s more, dogs and cats have short digestive tracts and are adapted to metabolize animal flesh, so proteins and fats are the preferred energy source for these animals — not carbs.

In terms of toxicity, however, there’s no issue if your pet consumes small amounts of barley, if necessary. Most people need to resort to adding grains to their pet food due to finances, and this is fine as long as it’s given in very small amounts. Don’t add grains “just because,” as there’s no taurine or other important nutrients found in carbs that pets lack.

Just like humans, pets can consume some foods that are metabolically stressful (fast foods, for example). However, the goal is to prioritize calories from healthy real foods that resonate with their innate metabolic machinery, particularly lean meats and healthy fats. Feeding a diet that contains less than 20% starchy carbs is the most nutritious, least metabolically stressful for dogs and cats.

Top Barley Producers in the US

In 2021, the U.S. produced 170.8 million bushels of barley. Idaho, Montana and North Dakota were the top producers, with Idaho’s production slightly higher than the two other states.4

Barley Contains Bioactive Phytochemicals

Giving small amounts of barley to your pet, such as using it as a food topper, can provide them with some nutrients, one example of which is phytochemicals. Flavonoids, phenolic acids and lignans are examples of phytochemicals found in barley. They have antioxidant, cholesterol-lowering and antiproliferative properties.

Phenolic acids are the most abundant group of phytochemicals in barley and are primarily located in the kernel’s outer layers. They’ve been linked to disease prevention and are an excellent source of antioxidants with antiradical and antiproliferative effects. Meanwhile, flavonoids have been linked to helping moderate many diseases including cancer and coronary heart diseases. Flavanols, anthocyanins and proanthocyanidins are the flavonoids found in barley.

Lignans, on the other hand, are natural defense substances found in plants that have antiviral, antioxidant, antibacterial and antitumor properties. They may help protect against coronary heart disease.5

Barley Also Has Fiber

A one-tablespoon serving of barley contains 0.37 grams of soluble fiber,6 which promotes smooth passage of food to the gastrointestinal (GI) tract. According to Harvard Health, the type of soluble fiber in barley is called beta glucans, which may have cholesterol-lowering abilities.7

Fiber is helpful for pets, as it builds the microbiome and provides roughage for bowel health. But remember that it should be provided in appropriate amounts only and not added to highly processed diets as a means of keeping stools artificially firm or tricking animals into thinking they are satiated.

If you’re feeding your dog or cat a nutritionally balanced, species-appropriate diet, which includes low-glycemic vegetables, along with appropriate supplementation, including pet probiotics and digestive enzymes, and they’re producing small, firm stools, then they’re getting the right amount of fiber they need.

Other Nutrients in Barley

B vitamins, particularly niacin (vitamin B3), thiamine (vitamin B1) and pyridoxine (vitamin B6), are found in barley.8 In pets, niacin is essential for maintaining your pet’s GI tract, nervous system tissue and skin function.9 Thiamine, meanwhile, is needed for normal growth, nerve impulse transmission and metabolism of carbohydrates.10 Pyridoxine is needed for producing red blood cells and neurotransmitters.11

In addition, barley contains minerals like iron and magnesium.12 Iron is crucial for metabolic function and oxygen transport in hemoglobin,13 while magnesium is needed for “bone mineralization, muscle contraction and relaxation, and neuronal signal transduction.”14

Beware of Foxtail Barley

Don’t confuse foxtail barley with the typical barley plant. A common type of weed, foxtail barley (Hordeum jubatum) can be dangerous to pets, as the bristles of the plant can get in their ears, eyes, mouth or paws. If you spot it while out on a walk with your pet, stay away.

Antinutrients in Barley

Despite having small amounts of the nutrients mentioned above, an important reason why you should limit barley and other lectin-containing grains in your pet’s diet is because they contain gluten, a naturally occurring protein that acts as a binder.15

Gluten is an antinutrient — this means it interferes with how the body absorbs important minerals and nutrients.16 Gluten can lead to intestinal permeability, where animals can develop inflammation in their intestines, leading to unpleasant symptoms such as weight loss, diarrhea and more.17

Lectins, on the other hand, are proteins that bind to carbohydrates and are found in animal studies to interfere with the absorption of minerals like iron, zinc and calcium. They can lead to side effects like nausea, diarrhea, stomach upset and inflammatory conditions.18

Aside from gluten, other antinutrients found in whole grains like barley are phytic acid and saponins.19,20 While there are ways to minimize these antinutrients through proper food preparation (for example, one study notes that soaking may help reduce the phytates in wheat and barley21), the best course of action is still to feed these grains, and all starchy carbs, in limited amounts to healthy animals — they should not make up a significant portion of your pet’s nutritionally balanced species-appropriate diet.

If your pet requires a lower protein diet that needs to include a starch, sprouted rolled oats provide a more nutritious and gluten-free, healthier alternative.

Sustainability of Barley

Barley is grown not just for food but also for erosion control. The plant’s roots grow deep into soil, giving it protection from factors that may contribute to erosion, such as wind and rain. For this reason, barley is usually planted as a cold-weather cover crop. The plant also releases nitrogen into the soil. Barley may also help reduce weeds by outcompeting and shading them.

Growing barley doesn’t take up a lot of water; it’s a low water-intensive crop. It uses 171 gallons of water per pound. This plant prefers dry, arid climates and is unable to stand heavy moisture in the soil.22

Unfortunately, conventionally grown barley is often contaminated with glyphosate,23 a carcinogenic active ingredient found in weedkillers such as Roundup. In grain crops like barley, wheat and oat, glyphosate is used as a desiccant, in order to speed up their harvest.24

In humans, glyphosate has been linked to adverse effects, like disrupting more than 50% of the microbiome, as well as increasing the risk of premature births, miscarriages and Non-Hodgkin’s lymphoma.25,26,27,28 Today, new studies are shedding light on its potential negative effects on companion animals. Aside from being detected in dogs’ and cats’ urine,29 a 2020 analysis observed its potential to cause different kinds of cancer, like hemangiosarcoma, in animals.30 To make sure you do not expose your family, including your pets, to glyphosate in barley, always buy organic varieties.

Remember — Do the Carb Equation When Feeding Dry Pet Food

Before purchasing any dry pet food, always do the carb equation to ensure your pet is receiving an adequate amount of meat-derived protein and not gluten-containing carbs that do nothing for your pet’s health. In some pet food labels, the carb content is intentionally left off to avoid "confusing" pet owners. Here's the formula to help you determine carb content:

100% - % protein - % fat - % moisture - % ash (if not listed, use 6%) = % carbs
Example, cat food: Royal Canin Indoor Adult Dry Cat Food
100% - 27% protein - 15% fat - 8% moisture - 6% ash = 44% carbs
Example, dog food: Royal Canin Medium Adult Dry Dog Food
100% - 23% protein - 12% fat - 10% moisture - 6% ash = 49% carbs

In these two examples, it's obvious that the amount of carbohydrates far exceeds the goal of keeping carbs to less than 20% of the diet. But even when fiber is accounted for, the bulk of calories in most dry pet foods come from unnecessary, high glycemic starch, which is not only metabolically stressful and biologically inappropriate but leads to a host of degenerative diseases over time. So while barley isn’t toxic for pets, remember to only feed sparsely and in moderation.

If you’re feeding dog food to your pets and check the ingredients on the label, you might see the word “barley” in the list. Barley, just like rice and other grains, is commonly added to most commercial dog foods, but what is this food actually? Can it provide your pets with notable benefits? Keep reading to discover what barley is, and whether or not it’s a good addition to your pet’s diet.

What Is Barley and Why Is It Used in Pet Foods?

Barley (Hordeum vulgare) belongs to the grass family Poaceae and is known for the edible grain it produces. It’s the fourth largest grain crop grown worldwide, after wheat, rice and corn.1 In the U.S., a large majority of the barley production goes into animal feed and beer manufacturing2 — hence the reason why you’ll see it in some conventional pet foods.

The reason why barley is used in pet foods is because it’s cheaper — it’s rich in carbohydrates, and these carb fillers allow the manufacturer to reduce the amount of meat, which is far more expensive, in their recipes.

Did You Know?

Barley has a long history of use. In ancient Mesopotamia, it was used as a form of currency. Pliny the Elder, a Roman historian, also wrote that in ancient Greece, this food was given to the gladiators, and they’re referred to as “barley eaters.”3

So Is Barley Good for Your Dogs and Cats?

The truth is that barley is a grain, just like wheat and rice. Dogs and cats have no biological need for carbs, and it only converts in their body to sugar. What’s more, dogs and cats have short digestive tracts and are adapted to metabolize animal flesh, so proteins and fats are the preferred energy source for these animals — not carbs.

In terms of toxicity, however, there’s no issue if your pet consumes small amounts of barley, if necessary. Most people need to resort to adding grains to their pet food due to finances, and this is fine as long as it’s given in very small amounts. Don’t add grains “just because,” as there’s no taurine or other important nutrients found in carbs that pets lack.

Just like humans, pets can consume some foods that are metabolically stressful (fast foods, for example). However, the goal is to prioritize calories from healthy real foods that resonate with their innate metabolic machinery, particularly lean meats and healthy fats. Feeding a diet that contains less than 20% starchy carbs is the most nutritious, least metabolically stressful for dogs and cats.

Top Barley Producers in the US

In 2021, the U.S. produced 170.8 million bushels of barley. Idaho, Montana and North Dakota were the top producers, with Idaho’s production slightly higher than the two other states.4

Barley Contains Bioactive Phytochemicals

Giving small amounts of barley to your pet, such as using it as a food topper, can provide them with some nutrients, one example of which is phytochemicals. Flavonoids, phenolic acids and lignans are examples of phytochemicals found in barley. They have antioxidant, cholesterol-lowering and antiproliferative properties.

Phenolic acids are the most abundant group of phytochemicals in barley and are primarily located in the kernel’s outer layers. They’ve been linked to disease prevention and are an excellent source of antioxidants with antiradical and antiproliferative effects. Meanwhile, flavonoids have been linked to helping moderate many diseases including cancer and coronary heart diseases. Flavanols, anthocyanins and proanthocyanidins are the flavonoids found in barley.

Lignans, on the other hand, are natural defense substances found in plants that have antiviral, antioxidant, antibacterial and antitumor properties. They may help protect against coronary heart disease.5

Barley Also Has Fiber

A one-tablespoon serving of barley contains 0.37 grams of soluble fiber,6 which promotes smooth passage of food to the gastrointestinal (GI) tract. According to Harvard Health, the type of soluble fiber in barley is called beta glucans, which may have cholesterol-lowering abilities.7

Fiber is helpful for pets, as it builds the microbiome and provides roughage for bowel health. But remember that it should be provided in appropriate amounts only and not added to highly processed diets as a means of keeping stools artificially firm or tricking animals into thinking they are satiated.

If you’re feeding your dog or cat a nutritionally balanced, species-appropriate diet, which includes low-glycemic vegetables, along with appropriate supplementation, including pet probiotics and digestive enzymes, and they’re producing small, firm stools, then they’re getting the right amount of fiber they need.

Other Nutrients in Barley

B vitamins, particularly niacin (vitamin B3), thiamine (vitamin B1) and pyridoxine (vitamin B6), are found in barley.8 In pets, niacin is essential for maintaining your pet’s GI tract, nervous system tissue and skin function.9 Thiamine, meanwhile, is needed for normal growth, nerve impulse transmission and metabolism of carbohydrates.10 Pyridoxine is needed for producing red blood cells and neurotransmitters.11

In addition, barley contains minerals like iron and magnesium.12 Iron is crucial for metabolic function and oxygen transport in hemoglobin,13 while magnesium is needed for “bone mineralization, muscle contraction and relaxation, and neuronal signal transduction.”14

Beware of Foxtail Barley

Don’t confuse foxtail barley with the typical barley plant. A common type of weed, foxtail barley (Hordeum jubatum) can be dangerous to pets, as the bristles of the plant can get in their ears, eyes, mouth or paws. If you spot it while out on a walk with your pet, stay away.

Antinutrients in Barley

Despite having small amounts of the nutrients mentioned above, an important reason why you should limit barley and other lectin-containing grains in your pet’s diet is because they contain gluten, a naturally occurring protein that acts as a binder.15

Gluten is an antinutrient — this means it interferes with how the body absorbs important minerals and nutrients.16 Gluten can lead to intestinal permeability, where animals can develop inflammation in their intestines, leading to unpleasant symptoms such as weight loss, diarrhea and more.17

Lectins, on the other hand, are proteins that bind to carbohydrates and are found in animal studies to interfere with the absorption of minerals like iron, zinc and calcium. They can lead to side effects like nausea, diarrhea, stomach upset and inflammatory conditions.18

Aside from gluten, other antinutrients found in whole grains like barley are phytic acid and saponins.19,20 While there are ways to minimize these antinutrients through proper food preparation (for example, one study notes that soaking may help reduce the phytates in wheat and barley21), the best course of action is still to feed these grains, and all starchy carbs, in limited amounts to healthy animals — they should not make up a significant portion of your pet’s nutritionally balanced species-appropriate diet.

If your pet requires a lower protein diet that needs to include a starch, sprouted rolled oats provide a more nutritious and gluten-free, healthier alternative.

Sustainability of Barley

Barley is grown not just for food but also for erosion control. The plant’s roots grow deep into soil, giving it protection from factors that may contribute to erosion, such as wind and rain. For this reason, barley is usually planted as a cold-weather cover crop. The plant also releases nitrogen into the soil. Barley may also help reduce weeds by outcompeting and shading them.

Growing barley doesn’t take up a lot of water; it’s a low water-intensive crop. It uses 171 gallons of water per pound. This plant prefers dry, arid climates and is unable to stand heavy moisture in the soil.22

Unfortunately, conventionally grown barley is often contaminated with glyphosate,23 a carcinogenic active ingredient found in weedkillers such as Roundup. In grain crops like barley, wheat and oat, glyphosate is used as a desiccant, in order to speed up their harvest.24

In humans, glyphosate has been linked to adverse effects, like disrupting more than 50% of the microbiome, as well as increasing the risk of premature births, miscarriages and Non-Hodgkin’s lymphoma.25,26,27,28 Today, new studies are shedding light on its potential negative effects on companion animals. Aside from being detected in dogs’ and cats’ urine,29 a 2020 analysis observed its potential to cause different kinds of cancer, like hemangiosarcoma, in animals.30 To make sure you do not expose your family, including your pets, to glyphosate in barley, always buy organic varieties.

Remember — Do the Carb Equation When Feeding Dry Pet Food

Before purchasing any dry pet food, always do the carb equation to ensure your pet is receiving an adequate amount of meat-derived protein and not gluten-containing carbs that do nothing for your pet’s health. In some pet food labels, the carb content is intentionally left off to avoid "confusing" pet owners. Here's the formula to help you determine carb content:

100% - % protein - % fat - % moisture - % ash (if not listed, use 6%) = % carbs
Example, cat food: Royal Canin Indoor Adult Dry Cat Food
100% - 27% protein - 15% fat - 8% moisture - 6% ash = 44% carbs
Example, dog food: Royal Canin Medium Adult Dry Dog Food
100% - 23% protein - 12% fat - 10% moisture - 6% ash = 49% carbs

In these two examples, it's obvious that the amount of carbohydrates far exceeds the goal of keeping carbs to less than 20% of the diet. But even when fiber is accounted for, the bulk of calories in most dry pet foods come from unnecessary, high glycemic starch, which is not only metabolically stressful and biologically inappropriate but leads to a host of degenerative diseases over time. So while barley isn’t toxic for pets, remember to only feed sparsely and in moderation.
